name: oneTBB
baseline: sequential libstdc++ STL algorithms (std::sort, std::for_each, std::transform, std::reduce, std::exclusive_scan, std::all_of, std::find_if)
workload: poolSTL's Google Benchmark suite on 100M-element int vectors (for_each and transform with a tiny per-element body, reduce, all_of, find_if, exclusive_scan) and std::sort on 10M random ints, comparing the plain sequential call with std::execution::par; on GCC the benchmark only builds the std::execution::par rows when it finds and links TBB::tbb, so those rows run on the oneTBB backend.
claimed_speedup: Indirect, via GCC std::execution::par on the oneTBB backend, M1 Pro 8 cores, times from the poolSTL README table: sort 603 ms sequential vs 113 ms (about 5.3x, derived from page data); for_each 94.6 ms vs 15.3 ms (about 6.2x, derived); transform 95.0 ms vs 15.3 ms (about 6.2x, derived); reduce 15.2 ms vs 3.38 ms (about 4.5x, derived); all_of 19.9 ms vs 3.45 ms (about 5.8x, derived); find_if at needle 50 percent 9.87 ms vs 1.75 ms (about 5.6x, derived); exclusive_scan 33.7 ms vs 19.8 ms (about 1.7x, derived). The oneTBB repo itself carries no benchmark and no speedup claim.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13 (README says only 'with GCC 13'); flags for the README run not stated; benchmark/CMakeLists.txt sets Release flags -g -O3 -DNDEBUG and links TBB::tbb for the std::execution::par rows; TBB version not stated.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (6 performance + 2 efficiency cores)
stars_or_usage: 6.8k stars; the repo now lives at uxlfoundation/oneTBB (oneapi-src/oneTBB redirects); the GCC and Clang parallel STL need TBB for std::execution::par (poolSTL README compatibility table)
tradeoffs: Extra link dependency (-ltbb) for the GCC and Clang parallel STL; a task-scheduler thread pool, so short sequences can lose to sequential code (the seed lead, from a C++ book, blames per-call thread start in the GCC and Clang integration; not verified here); unrelated to the Rust or OpenMP schedulers, with its own work-stealing arena model.
caveats: Indirect and third-party: the numbers measure libstdc++'s parallel STL running on oneTBB (std::execution::par), not the tbb:: API directly, and were produced by the author of poolSTL, a competing library, whose README does not say the TBB backend was linked for that run (inferred from the benchmark CMake logic) nor the build type or TBB version. One machine, 8 heterogeneous cores, so the speedup is not scaling data; for_each and transform bodies are almost empty. exclusive_scan gains only 1.7x. Counter-evidence: in the PPQSort README (Fujitsu A64FX, 48 cores, 2e9 ints) oneTBB parallel_sort took 43.66 s on random input against 5.84 s for PPQSort and 13.72 s for GCC's OpenMP parallel-mode quicksort, and ranked 9th of 9 on the total (118.23 s); that table has no sequential row. oneTBB 2023.2 release notes say parallel_sort was 'significantly improved' with a parallel partitioning step, with no numbers. No direct oneTBB vs OpenMP vs std::thread table was found: README, RELEASE_NOTES.md, test/ and rfcs/ of the repo have no benchmark data (there is no benchmark/ directory on master, the URL returns 404), and the book lead credits no TBB numbers. Web search snippets (pages not opened) showed only old forum posts, for example a Core 2 Quad parallel_sort test with serial 2.545 s against 1.07 s on 4 threads.
found_via: seed-record pass, starting from https://github.com/oneapi-src/oneTBB (README, RELEASE_NOTES.md, test/, rfcs/ checked; no in-tree benchmark); WebSearch 'oneTBB parallel_sort speedup over std::sort' surfaced the PPQSort README; poolSTL README benchmark section (std::execution::par vs sequential) gave the numbers.

name: Rayon
baseline: OpenMP parallel for (C++ with static and dynamic scheduling)
workload: Fork Union README Performance section: N-body at 512 bodies on every logical core (microseconds per iteration, static / dynamic) and connected components by label propagation on a ~27M-edge R-MAT community graph (GTEPS, 84 fork-join rounds per pass), 30-second window per cell, four machines; Rayon par_iter_mut with static chunks or unit grain against OpenMP in C++.
claimed_speedup: Mixed, mostly OpenMP ahead. Rayon wins: N-body on the 24x Intel RPL Windows box, Rayon 151 / 151 us vs OpenMP 360 / 627 us (about 2.4x static, 4.2x dynamic, derived from page data); connected components with dynamic scheduling, Rayon vs OpenMP GTEPS 6.5 vs 0.4 on 128x Intel SPR (about 16x, derived), 6.2 vs 0.4 on 192x Graviton 5 (about 15x, derived), 5.2 vs 0.1 on 24x Intel RPL (about 50x from rounded values, derived); static connected components on 18x Apple M5 Pro 23.8 vs 23.0 (about 1.03x, derived). Rayon loses: N-body on M5 Pro 222 / 339 us vs 115 / 137, on SPR 483 / 739 vs 115 / 226, on Graviton 5 490 / 580 vs 266 / 216; static connected components on SPR 8.5 vs 28.2 GTEPS, on Graviton 5 8.4 vs 53.9, on RPL 9.4 vs 11.4.
compiler_and_flags: C++ side: -O3 -march=native, no LTO, with -ffast-math, built with LLVM clang plus libomp per the scripts/nbody.cpp header (compiler versions not stated; the README names MinGW-GCC for the Windows i9 box); run under numactl --interleave=all with OMP_PROC_BIND=spread OMP_PLACES=cores. Rust side: cargo build --release with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native', no LTO, unchecked hot loops, rayon 1.11 requirement in Cargo.toml.
hardware: 18x Apple M5 Pro (macOS); 24x Intel RPL (Windows, also called a 24x i9 in the README); 128x Intel SPR (Linux); 192x AWS Graviton 5 (Linux); exact CPU SKUs not given
tradeoffs: Rust-only (C++ projects must call it over FFI or rewrite the loop); par_iter is a one-line change and the API guarantees data-race freedom; dynamic splitting by default means no static schedule, so uniform loops pay stealing overhead and tiny per-item work can run slower than serial (forum reports, not opened).
caveats: Evidence is a side result of a competing library's benchmark: the README belongs to Fork Union (ForkUnion, Rust and C++), whose author promotes it as 3-6x faster than OpenMP and 12-16x faster than Rayon, so the figures were not produced by the Rayon project and a verifier may prefer tier C. Rayon beats OpenMP only in a minority of cells; OpenMP's 'dynamic' columns use a one-vertex grain that makes its shared queue collapse (0.1-0.4 GTEPS), which is why the 15-50x Rayon wins appear; against OpenMP's static schedule Rayon is behind on most machines (up to 6.4x lower GTEPS on Graviton 5). The one N-body win is on the Windows box where the README names MinGW-GCC for C++, so the OpenMP runtime there is probably libgomp, not libomp. The C++ build adds -ffast-math, which Rust cannot express globally (kernels reduce in a fixed order to compensate, per the source comment). Exact CPU models and compiler versions are not given and the benchmark does not use the cited 'oneTBB parallel_for' or 'std::execution::par' baselines. Rayon's own repo has no comparison against OpenMP, TBB or std::execution::par: README, FAQ.md and RELEASES.md carry no numbers, PR #1156 (par_sort sync) says 'mostly the same or slightly better' with no figures, and rayon-demo prints sequential-vs-parallel speedups at run time without stored results. A search snippet (arXiv 2502.15536, NPB-Rust, page blocked and not opened) reports Rayon slower than C++ OpenMP on the NAS kernels; snippet only.
found_via: seed-record pass, starting from https://github.com/rayon-rs/rayon (README, FAQ.md, RELEASES.md, rayon-demo checked, no cross-library numbers); WebSearch 'Rust rayon vs C++ OpenMP vs oneTBB parallel_for benchmark' surfaced the Fork Union / 'beyond openmp in cpp rust' material; the Fork Union README Performance tables carry the Rayon and OpenMP columns.

name: uberlog
baseline: synchronous write-per-message file logging (a 'naive logging system' that issues one OS write call per message)
workload: README Benchmarks: time taken inside the calling program to format a roughly 200-byte message and push it into the shared-memory ring buffer (200 ns Windows, 280 ns Linux), against a hypothetical naive logger costing about 1500 ns for a 100-byte write() plus an assumed 1000 ns of formatting.
claimed_speedup: README: 200 ns (Windows) and 280 ns (Linux) per formatted message, 350 MB/s and 465 MB/s throughput, versus about 2500 ns per message for a naive write-per-message logger, 'a 10x speedup over a naive system'; at 100000 messages per second the naive logger spends 25% of time logging against 2% for uberlog. Ratios derived from page data: 2500/280 is about 8.9x on Linux and 2500/200 is 12.5x on Windows.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the README numbers. The repo build script uses clang++ -O2 -ggdb -std=c++11 on Linux and macOS; an msvc/ project covers Windows.
tradeoffs: Multi-process design: a spawned child process (uberlogger) drains a shared-memory ring buffer and writes the file, so a crash in the main process still flushes earlier messages; the caller stalls only when the ring is full. Adds a second process and shared memory; fixed log line format unless you derive from Logger; printf-compatible type-safe formatting (tsf); log rolling built in; C++11.
caveats: The baseline is hypothetical, not a measured run: the 2500 ns figure adds a quoted ~1500 ns write() cost to an assumed 1000 ns of formatting. test.cpp does time a 5-byte write() (BenchFileWriteLatency) and the logger latency modes, but no result file is stored. test.cpp also has a 'spd comparison' benchmark that only times 1M uberlog Info() calls and contains no spdlog code; there are no spdlog numbers anywhere in the repo or issues (0 issues). Third-party logging shootouts found (MuggleWei cc_log_benchmark) do not list uberlog. Latency counts only the in-program cost, not the writer process's work. README itself says a naive logger is fine below many thousands of messages per second, and the 2018 Meltdown/KPTI benefit is 'not measured'. The seed lead (from a C++ book) says it is not as fast as specialized low-latency loggers. No commits since 2020-04-08 (over 3 years).
found_via: seed-record pass, starting from https://github.com/IMQS/uberlog (README Benchmarks section, test.cpp, build script); WebSearch 'IMQS uberlog benchmark spdlog comparison latency' found no third-party comparison.
